title: Karmic tail 12-16-4 in the destiny matrix: the Emperor, the calm before the storm and power without a fist

seo.title: Karmic Tail 12-16-4 “The Emperor”: Meaning in the Destiny Matrix
seo.description: 12-16-4 is the tail of a power that holds everything, even the person, until lightning strikes. A ten-second date check, Strength in the centre, seven practices.

short: 12-16-4 is the karmic tail that popular destiny matrix readings call “the Emperor” (less often, “the Ruler”). Its script is a power that holds everything, including the person themselves. First the person holds themselves back: stays silent, puts things off, says “I’ll sort it out later”. The tension builds up and one day discharges in a collapse: an ultimatum, a break-up, walking out overnight. After the collapse they build a new order, stricter than the last, and the circle starts again. The Hanged Man (12) opens the circle — hands tied behind the back. The Tower (16) holds it: change comes only with lightning. At the root stands the Emperor (4): the task of learning a kind of power that doesn’t need total control. One person in sixteen has this tail. And everyone who has it has the same hidden fourth card in the centre of the chart — Strength: a woman closing a lion’s jaws without a fist. So the main question of the tail is not “hold on or let go” but what to hold with.

sections.h2: Do you have the 12-16-4 tail: a ten-second check
paragraphs: You don’t need a calculator. The 12-16-4 tail comes up if, and only if, the first three numbers of the matrix add up to **31 or 40**. There is also one single date with the sum 4 — 1 January 2000.

ol: **Day arcanum** — your day of birth. If it is greater than 22, add its digits: 23 → 5, 29 → 11, 31 → 4.
**Year arcanum** — the sum of the digits of the year. If the result is greater than 22, add the digits again: 1985 → 23 → 5, while 1990 → 19.

paragraphs: Add up the three numbers. If you get 31 or 40, you have 12-16-4. Any other result means a different tail.

ul: 11.12.1978: 11 + 12 + 7 = 30 → not this one (this date has the 9-12-3 tail).
31.03.1993: 4 + 3 + 22 = 29 → not this one (this date has the 15-8-11 tail).

paragraphs: If your chart is already calculated, it is even simpler. Look at the bottom corner — point D, the “karmic task”. If it holds 4, the tail is 12-16-4, without exception.

Why this works. The sum of the three numbers reduces into the bottom corner of the chart: 31 → 3 + 1 = 4, 40 → 4 + 0 = 4. So D = 4 — the Emperor. The centre E is the same sum plus the corner: 31 + 4 = 35 → 8, 40 + 4 = 44 → 8. After that there are no options left: the entry M = 4 + 8 = 12, the middle N = 4 + 12 = 16. There are no other routes to 12-16-4. This was checked by going through all 73,414 days from 1900 to 2100.
Read the scheme from the bottom up: this is the tower itself.

All four numbers are multiples of four: 4, 8, 12, 16. Each floor is the previous one plus one more four of the Emperor. The tail is literally built from his bricks. What follows from this is covered below, in the section on the hidden card.
The same arithmetic leads to facts you won’t find in popular readings:

ul: **One person in sixteen has it.** Among birth dates from 1940 to 2012, 12-16-4 accounts for 6.4%. That is 6th place out of 26 possible tails.
**This is a tail of the parents’ generation, not the children’s.** The later the year of birth, the rarer it is:

paragraphs: The reason is arithmetic. Years of the 2000s have a small arcanum (2000 → 2, 2010 → 3), so to make it up to 31 the day and month have to be large. Among people born from 2000 to 2025, 12-16-4 is only thirteenth in frequency.

ul: **The number of such days depends almost entirely on the year.** The most are in 1963, 1972, 1981 and 1990 — 35 each. Among people born in 1990, almost one in ten has 12-16-4. The fewest — 7 days each — are in 2000, 2001 and 2010, and 1967, 1976, 1985 and 1994 have only 9 each.
**The Emperor at the root always means this tail.** The bottom corners 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 each give two different tails. The four has only one option.

**4-16-12 is the same tail.** If you see 4, 16 and 12 on the bottom ray of your chart, you are reading the same tail from the outer corner towards the centre. No tail in this scheme begins with 4: the inner point M is always a multiple of three.

sections.h2: Why this tail is called “the Emperor”
paragraphs: Popular readings explain the name with a past-life legend. The legend has two versions, and they are opposites. In the first, the person held power and abused it: gave orders, suppressed, controlled, could use force, and the people around them lived in fear. In the second, on the contrary, they were weak, didn’t take responsibility, submitted — and their life fell apart. Hence what is attributed to the tail today: “soft on the outside, iron will inside”, a habit of deciding for others or, on the contrary, the role of the ever-accommodating person who works for years under an unfair boss. The legend cannot be checked, and the numbers say nothing about past events. But its two versions are more accurate than they seem. They are not two different people but two phases of one circle.

The cards themselves support the name. Wen’s Emperor wears armour under his red robe: this suggests “a warrior king”. The person who draws the card “possesses an iron will”, and the card says: “All is in order, under control.” The landscape behind the throne is dry, jagged rocks — according to Wen, a sign of “a stern, severe nature”. There is a coincidence in Waite’s divinatory lists too. The word “tyranny” belongs to the Tower: the meanings of the reversed card are “oppression, imprisonment, tyranny”. And “despotism, abuse of power” belong to Strength, which stands in the centre for this tail. These are meanings of reversed cards in a Tarot spread: numbers calculated from a date have no reversed position. But the vocabulary of tyranny in Waite’s book stands two steps away from this tail.

There is also an image that seems drawn for it. Waite lists the old names of the Tower. One of them is the Tower of Babel, and in this reading the figures falling from it are held to be “Nimrod and his minister”. Nimrod, according to legend, is the king who started building that tower. On the Waite–Smith card lightning strikes the top of the tower and knocks off its crown. Wen reads the falling crown as the toppling of materialistic ambitions. In this tail the crown is worn by the Emperor, and the lightning comes to where he sits highest of all.
Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the destiny matrix, so this is no proof of the name. But there are many coincidences.

sections.h2: How the circle works: the calm, the lightning, a new order
paragraphs: **1. Entry: the Hanged Man ties his own hands.** The script begins not with power but with its opposite: the person holds themselves back. They don’t argue, though they disagree. They don’t ask, though they need to. They don’t leave, though they have long felt cramped. They put their own things off “until better times” and answer “how are you?” with “fine”. In the old description of the card that Waite cites, the hanged man’s arms are bound behind him. Wen notes that his hands are hidden: “his ultimate offering to the world has yet to be seen”. On the outside all is calm. Wen calls this state “the unsettling calm before a storm”. For her, the storm is the next card of the deck, Death. In this tail, the Tower stands behind the calm.

An important detail. Waite insists that the hanged man’s tree is living, with leaves on it, and that his face “expresses deep entrancement, not suffering”. It is “life in suspension, but life and not death”. The Hanged Man’s pause is there to see the situation in a new way. The tail’s script understands it differently: as a duty to endure.

**2. Mechanism: the Tower discharges the tension.** What has gone unsaid does not disappear. It builds up until it finds a way out. For the people around, that way out is always sudden; for the person themselves, never. A resignation letter on Monday after three years of “fine”. “I’m filing for divorce” over a broken cup. A shout you are ashamed of for a week. Sometimes the blow comes from outside: what the person has propped up with themselves for years collapses — a project, an agreement, a relationship that rested on their silence. Waite calls the Tower a card “of unforeseen catastrophe”. In this tail, the catastrophe is unforeseen only by others.

For Waite, the Tower is not just destruction but the fall of a house built on a false foundation, “a House of Falsehood”. He recalls the line of the psalm: “except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.” Wen says the same thing more practically: “What seemed stable and solid to the Seeker is not so; it is in fact destructible and will come to destruction if the Seeker does not make drastic changes.” What is false in this house? Our answer: the two phrases it stood on — “I’m fine” and “everything is under control”. The lightning strikes exactly at them. Then come relief and the truth (“The aftermath is truth,” Wen writes), and along with them, fear and shame about what was destroyed.

**3. Root: the Emperor builds a new order.** The person climbs out from under the rubble with one decision: it will never be like this again. And they build again, harder than before: with rules, checks, reserves, keeping everything in their own hands. Waite calls the Emperor “executive and realization, the power of this world”, “the lordship of thought”. And he adds at once: this is not yet the wisdom which draws from a higher world.

To the person who draws the Emperor, Wen puts the most uncomfortable question: “what is the Seeker’s dominion? What has the Seeker conquered? The kingdom is parched.” The dry landscape, in her words, betrays a thirst for a different kind of sovereignty than the one the person has already attained. Wen also recalls King Midas. Everything he touched turned to gold, and he died of hunger, because gold cannot nourish. He turned his beloved daughter to gold too. An order that rests on control alone turns the living into the motionless. That is the task the root of the tail sets: learning a kind of power that does not scorch the earth around it.

**4. Repeat: one more floor.** After a collapse a person usually makes themselves one of two promises. The first: “Nobody will ever order me around again.” Control turns outwards, and the person becomes an Emperor for others. The second: “I’ll never lose it like that again.” Control turns inwards, and the person ties their own hands again, even tighter than before. The promises seem opposite but are made of the same material — power, the Emperor’s four. So both lead to the same place: a new pause, new tension and new lightning. Each turn adds another floor to the tower.

Imagine the head of a small team. For three years he plugs other people’s gaps, doesn’t argue with the director about deadlines and answers “how are you?” with “fine”. On Friday the director, in passing, moves his holiday — for the third time. On Monday there is a resignation letter on the desk, and everyone is surprised: he never complained. At the new job, from day one, he sets hard rules: everything goes through him, not a single decision without his approval, “I’ve had enough of that once already”. A year later his new team sits silent at meetings and answers “how’s it going?” with “fine”. The Tower hasn’t gone anywhere. It has moved, and now other people live in it.

sections.h2: The Obliging One, the Strict One and the Blast: one and the same tail
paragraphs: Popular readings describe 12-16-4 sometimes as a tyrant, sometimes as a victim. Wen gives this swinging a precise name. The hanged man’s crossed legs, she writes, form a tau cross — a sign of “the balance between dominion and slavery”. That is the scale this tail swings on. The Obliging One, the Strict One and the Blast are not three types of people but three phases of one script. Many go through all three in a lifetime, and some within a week.

paragraphs: The Obliging One and the Strict One often live in the same person, just in different places. At work he is obliging to the boss, at home he is strict with the family. Or the other way round: at the office he keeps everyone under his thumb, and at home he has been silent for years. The lightning usually strikes where the person was most obliging: that is where it built up longest.

This tail has one more treacherous property: it can hand roles over. If you hold the power, the other person gets the pause. A strict parent raises an obliging child; next to an obliging partner there is a strict one. Someone who hung upside down for years can easily hang others up once they get the sceptre.

sections.h2: The hidden fourth card: everyone with 12-16-4 has Strength in the centre
paragraphs: Everyone who has the 12-16-4 tail has 8, Strength, in the centre of the matrix. This is not a coincidence but arithmetic. The centre always reduces to 8, and the method derives the entry of the tail from it. In the method, the centre is the comfort zone, the point a person returns to. And the formulas of the tail add up almost to a sentence:

ul: **Strength = the Emperor + the Emperor** (4 + 4 = 8): power turned on oneself.
**The Hanged Man = the Emperor + Strength** (4 + 8 = 12): power over oneself taken as far as tied hands.
**The Tower = the Emperor + the Hanged Man** (4 + 12 = 16): control plus restraint give a discharge.

paragraphs: There is a fourth formula too. The energy chart shows it: everyone with this tail has Manipura, the row of will, status and money, equal to 8-8-16. **Strength + Strength = the Tower.** Self-restraint added to self-restraint gives lightning. This is perhaps the shortest description of the whole tail.

What does Strength itself look like? In Waite, a woman is closing a lion’s jaws. He makes a special point of how his design differs from the older pictures: her “beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers”. The lion, in one of Waite’s readings, is the passions, and the woman is “the higher nature in its liberation”. The chain of flowers signifies “the sweet yoke and the light burden” of Divine Law, “when it has been taken into the heart of hearts”. And an important caveat: the card, according to Waite, has nothing to do with self-confidence in the ordinary sense. Wen puts it more simply: “Compassion is strength.” You cannot impose your will on others by brute force; only “gentle, subtle influence” works. Strength, for her, is mastery over your own fears. For comparison she takes the Chariot: it gives the strength to master the world around you, while Strength gives the strength to master yourself.

Wen also describes how this card is distorted in a spread. There are two distortions, and they are opposite. The first is brute force, stubbornness, obstinacy. The second is holding back: the person “is holding back, and as a result is unable to achieve his or her objective”. Once again, this is a caveat about a reversed card in a Tarot spread, not about a calculated number. But the two distortions of Strength match the two modes of the tail exactly, the Strict One and the Obliging One. Strength in the centre is the point of balance between them.

What follows is our conclusion, not a quote. There are two ways to close a lion’s jaws. The first is by force: clamp the jaws shut and lock the beast in a tower. That is the path of the Hanged Man. The lion in the tower does not disappear; it grows and one day breaks the walls. That is the Tower. The second way is the one on the card: the lion is already tamed and walks alongside on a chain of flowers. Anger, desire and will don’t go anywhere. They are heard and led, not strangled. It is the same with other people: power rests not on fear but on an agreement that has been accepted with the heart. A chain of flowers is rules that people accept for themselves, not ones they put up with. The key to the tail is not giving up power. The key is changing what it is made of: an open palm instead of a sceptre.

sections.h2: Where else the tail sounds: two Towers and the Hanged Man in the line of love
paragraphs: The arithmetic of the tail places its cards in other spots of the matrix too. Here is what all its holders have in common, without exception:

**Two Towers.** The Tower stands in the middle of the tail and once more in Manipura’s Emotions. In actions and motivation, Strength is here: gentle persistence, the ability to carry a load and not break down. But a setback in your affairs is experienced as the Tower: as a lightning strike after which you can see what stood on a false foundation. The risk is the same as for the whole tail: a softness that keeps everything inside until a small refusal hits like thunder.
**The whole foundation.** All four cards of the tail stand in the three lower rows of the energy chart: Muladhara, Svadhisthana and Manipura. The tail lies at the base of the chart.

**The Hanged Man in the line of love.** The entry of the tail, point M, also opens the relationship line. So for everyone with 12-16-4 the line of love also begins with the Hanged Man. And for those born in 2009 or 2018 it repeats the tail entirely: 12-16-4.

**A mirror for those born in April.** Everyone with 12-16-4 born in April has the talent line on the top ray equal to 4-16-12: the same three cards in reverse order. This is not a second tail but a different position, and it should be read as talent. Our reading: the ability to build, to rebuild after a collapse and to look at a situation from another side can become their life’s work.
The scenes below are made-up examples, not a description of every person with this tail.

Here the tail has a real gift. People with 12-16-4 often become a load-bearing wall: a department, a family business, a project rests on them. They know how to build a system, take responsibility and see things through to a result. In Waite’s divinatory list the Emperor has “stability, power, protection, realization”. And they act better than most during a collapse: when everything is falling apart, they already know what to do, because they have seen it more than once.

The trap lies in the same load-bearing wall. “It’s easier to do it myself”, “without me it will fall apart”, twenty sign-offs for one decision. The people around gradually stop taking the initiative: why bother, if it will all be redone anyway. There is a mirror version too. Years under a harsh boss, overtime without objection, a promotion never once asked for — and then walking out overnight, with no plan, slamming the door. Both versions are inside the circle.

Money in this tail is above all a defence against helplessness: a cushion, control over spending, “I’ve got it all worked out”. It is a support until it turns into Midas’s gold: the money piles up but spending it is frightening, or control over spending becomes power over loved ones. Sharp money moves often happen after a long pause, when the tension has nowhere left to go: quitting without a backup plan, investing everything at once, selling in a single day. The numbers do not predict this. But if it rings true, the strong move is simple: talk about money early and a little at a time. Ask for a raise when you have earned it, not when the resignation letter is already written.

In a couple this tail is recognised by the phrase the partner says after the explosion: “But you never said anything!” For years the person adjusts. Agrees to the other’s choice of holiday, the other’s relatives every Sunday, the other’s way of running the house. It seems to them that they are protecting the relationship. In fact they are running up a bill the partner doesn’t even know about. Then — a broken cup or being half an hour late, and there is a suitcase by the door.

The other side of the tail is the Emperor at home. “I know better how it should be done”, decisions for two, care that looks like guardianship. Next to such a partner, the other person gradually falls silent — and starts hanging upside down themselves. This is the same swing between “dominion and slavery” that Wen writes about, only for two. And in such a couple the Tower often comes from the side of the one who stayed silent.

Strength suggests a third way: stay in touch with a strong feeling without suppressing either it or the other person. Say “this doesn’t work for me” on the very first evening, not three years later. Ask instead of waiting for them to guess. And remember the difference: to care means to ask what suits the other person, not to decide for them. Imagine a couple choosing where to live. The weak version of the tail either silently agrees and then can’t forgive for years, or decides everything for both in advance: “I’ve already paid the deposit.” The strong version says: “This matters to me, and this is what I’m afraid of. What are you afraid of?”

A parent with 12-16-4 easily becomes an Emperor for their child: rules, control, “as long as you live under my roof”. The child learns one of two things: to hang, that is, to stay silent and adjust, or to explode. Teenage rebellion in such a family often looks like the Tower: years of quiet, then everything at once. If you were raised this way yourself and this rings true, notice where you are repeating a familiar order, and where a familiar silence. The most honest question for such a parent: can your child say “no” to you and feel safe?

sections.h2: Order or control, a pause or getting stuck: how to tell them apart
paragraphs: Each card of the tail has a healthy version and a script version. From the outside they are easy to confuse.
**Order or control (the Emperor):**

ul: Can you explain why this rule is needed — not “that’s the way it’s done”, but how exactly it helps?
What will happen if it isn’t followed for a week? If the answer is “everything will collapse”, check whether that is true.
Can anyone other than you change this rule?
Do you feel calmer when the people around you know what to expect, or when they do exactly what you said?

paragraphs: **A pause or getting stuck (the Hanged Man):**

ul: Does your pause have a deadline or a condition under which it will end?
Are you waiting to understand the situation better, or for it to resolve itself?
Does anyone besides you know that something isn’t working for you?
Does your view of the situation change during the pause? Or do you think the same thought day after day?

paragraphs: **Rebuilding or a collapse (the Tower):**

ul: Can what is in the way be taken apart piece by piece, without destroying everything?
Are you making the decision at the peak of your anger or after it?
Did things get better after the last “that’s it, enough”? Or did the same thing happen again in a new place?
What from the old will you take with you when you build the new?

sections.h2: What to do with the 12-16-4 tail: seven practices
paragraphs: These are the author’s exercises, drawn from the logic of the trio — not a ritual and not a guarantee of results.

ol: **Audit the tower.** Write down the rules you hold to: at work, at home, in how you treat yourself. “I check everything myself”, “the house has to be like this”, “I don’t complain”. For each rule, answer three questions: when did it appear, what does it protect against, and what will happen if you loosen it by a tenth. Choose one rule and revisit it out loud with the people it affects.

**Small lightning.** Discontent you kept quiet about becomes a brick in the wall. Take on a 24-hour rule: say “this doesn’t work for me” within 24 hours, in one sentence, in a calm voice. A small discharge on time replaces a big one three years later.

**Repair instead of demolition.** When you want to leave, break off, tear everything down, first name one thing that can be changed this week, and do it. But don’t turn repair into a new round of enduring: set a date. If nothing has moved by then, decide — but calmly, not at the peak of your anger.

**The sceptre on loan.** Hand over one area completely: the budget for a trip, redecorating a room, a small project. Hand it over along with the right to make mistakes. Agree with yourself not to interfere for a month, and notice the anxiety that will raise its head. That is the lion that needs to be led, not locked up.

**A chain of flowers.** Replace one order with an agreement. Not “do it this way”, but “here’s what matters to me; how would you like to get there?” A rule that was worked out together holds without supervision. A rule that was imposed holds only while you are watching.

**Hands out from behind the back.** In Wen, the hanged man’s hands are hidden, and his ultimate offering to the world has yet to be seen. Find one thing of your own that you put off “until better times”, and take the first step this week. And ask for help with one specific thing. Don’t hint — ask directly.

**First the lion, then the words.** When anger rises, don’t stifle it and don’t spill it out. Name it to yourself: “I’m angry because…”. Let your body live it through: a brisk walk, the stairs, sport. And only then speak. The goal is not to crush the feeling but to make sure it doesn’t decide for you.

paragraphs: And five phrases that break the script in the moment:

ul: Instead of “fine” — “this doesn’t work for me”.
Instead of “I’ll do it myself” — “please take this part”.
Instead of “that’s it, I’ve had enough” — “let’s change this by the end of the month”.
Instead of “because I said so” — “here’s why this rule exists. What about it is awkward for you?”
Instead of “never again” — “next time I’ll speak up sooner”.

sections.h2: The strength of 12-16-4: power that people follow without fear
paragraphs: A worked-through 12-16-4 gives a rare combination. The person knows how to hold a structure (the Emperor), how to stop and look at a situation differently (the Hanged Man) and how to take apart what has outlived itself before it gets torn down (the Tower). Such people are the best in a crisis. They know what a collapse looks like from the inside, they don’t panic and they know how to restore things. They build systems in which people feel calm: the rules are clear and can be discussed. Their power rests not on fear but on trust. In Waite’s divinatory list, Strength has the word “magnanimity”, and the Emperor has “protection” and “aid”.

Even the Tower works for the person in the worked-through tail. Wen sets it apart from Judgement: the Tower’s revelation leads not to the end of the road but “to rebuilding and reconstruction”. “The old must be destroyed so that the new can be built, this time correctly and for the right reasons.” A worked-through 12-16-4 does this demolition itself, of its own free will, piece by piece and on time. It no longer needs the lightning: it holds the tool itself.

The Emperor’s parched kingdom has a detail that is easy to miss. Wen describes it like this: a small stream runs at the foot of the canyon. Even in the most tightly controlled kingdom, life flows — just down below, under the stones. The work of this tail is not to conquer more land. It is to let the water through. Then the kingdom won’t need lightning to change.

sections.h2: What this article is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M. The relationship line: M–R1–R, where L = C + E, R = L + M, R1 = M + R. The talent line: B–P–K, where K = B + E, P = B + K. Every sum greater than 22 is reduced by adding its digits. All numerical facts in the article were obtained by going through all 73,414 dates from 1900 to 2100 and checked against the calculator’s engine: the “31 or 40” condition, the constant centre 8, Manipura 8-8-16, frequencies by decade, the number of days by year, the matches with the relationship and talent lines.

**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922) and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Quotes are given in the original English. Nimrod in the Tower is one of the old interpretations that Waite retells, not his own explanation of the card.

**The name “the Emperor” and the past-life legend** come from popular destiny matrix readings. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the matrix or karmic tails. Putting the three cards together into a script, reading the centre as the key, and the “tower of fours” are the author’s interpretation.
This is an esoteric model for self-reflection, not a forecast, a diagnosis or advice on health, money or relationships.

faq.q: What happened in a past life of someone with the 12-16-4 tail?
faq.a: Popular readings speak of a person with power — a ruler, a military commander, the head of a clan — who abused it: suppressed, controlled, could use force. There is a reverse version too: the person was weak, avoided responsibility, and their life fell apart. This is a legend of the tradition: neither numbers nor cards establish events of past lives. It is more useful to read both versions as two phases of what is already visible now: a power that sometimes squeezes others and sometimes ties the person’s own hands.

Yes, if 4, 16 and 12 stand on the bottom ray of your chart: you have simply read the tail from the outer corner towards the centre. In the calculation it is written from the inner point M to the corner D. M is always a multiple of three (3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 or 21), so there is no tail that begins with 4. But if 4-16-12 stands on the top ray, it is the talent line. Everyone with the 12-16-4 tail who was born in April has it there. That is a different position and a different reading. In search, both versions are written with spaces: “12 16 4” and “4 16 12”.

faq.q: Does the Tower in the tail mean I am heading for a crash, bankruptcy or loss?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events, money or health. The Tower here describes how change happens for the person: not gradually but all at once, after a long build-up. It is a property of the script, not a date on the calendar. And that is exactly what can be changed: changes made on time and piece by piece don’t need lightning.

faq.q: How is 12-16-4 different from 12-19-7 — isn’t the entry the same?
faq.a: Both tails begin with the Hanged Man, but they hold it differently. In 12-19-7 the person gives themselves to a cause, and the pause is paid off by victory — the Sun. In 12-16-4 the person holds themselves back, and the pause discharges in a collapse — the Tower. Their roots are different too (the Chariot and the Emperor), as are their centres (the Hierophant and Strength). Telling them apart by date is simple. Add up the day arcanum, the month number and the year arcanum: 25, 34 or 43 give 12-19-7, while 31 or 40 give 12-16-4.

faq.q: Why do readings of this tail say so much about the father?
faq.a: The Emperor is traditionally a father figure. Wen writes that in the old tradition this card, in a woman’s reading, meant a father figure, and in a man’s, self-mastery. She herself suggests reading the card without reference to gender: as order and authority. The cards say nothing about what your father was like. But the first “emperor” a person meets is whoever set the rules at home, father or mother. If the theme rings true, it is useful to ask yourself whose order you are repeating. Or under whose order you are still hanging.

faq.q: Is 12-16-4 different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Gender plays no part in the calculation. In popular readings you can read that a woman with this tail “takes on male roles” and needs to “become softer and more feminine”, while a man needs to become “calmer and more patient”. These are stereotypes: power, order and responsibility don’t belong to one gender, any more than restraint belongs to the other. The task is the same for everyone: to hold without a fist.

faq.q: “The Emperor” — does that mean I’m a tyrant?
faq.a: No. The tail describes a person’s relationship with power, and many people with 12-16-4 have more of the Obliging One than of the Strict One in their lives. The anger attributed to the tail is more often suppressed than spilled out. That is exactly why it builds up until the Tower. If there is violence in your relationship, whichever side it comes from, the tail has nothing to do with it. This needs to be dealt with together with a specialist, and if you are under threat, turn to those who can protect you.

faq.q: Are the 12-16-4 tail and the “12-16-4 programme” the same thing?
faq.a: A karmic tail is only the trio on the bottom ray, between the centre and the bottom corner of the chart. In this scheme the same numbers occur in one more place — the relationship line. For holders of the tail born in 2009 or 2018, the relationship line repeats the tail entirely. For some people born in 1931 and 1940 the relationship line is also 12-16-4, but their tail is different — 12-19-7. In the money channel and the talent line the 12-16-4 trio never occurs at all. If the numbers stand anywhere other than the bottom ray, read them by the meaning of that position.

The numbers in the matrix don’t change; what changes is how the script plays out. Signs of a worked-through tail: you speak about discontent while it is still small; your pauses have deadlines; you change what doesn’t work piece by piece and on time; your rules can be discussed; the people around you don’t fall silent. Lightning stops being the only way to change.

faq.q: What should I do if my child has 12-16-4?
faq.a: Give them power that fits their size: choosing their clothes, managing their own pocket money, being responsible for their own task — and the right to make mistakes in all of it. Let them be angry in words: “I’m angry because…”, without punishing them for the anger itself. Don’t break their will: the lion on the Strength card follows the woman on a chain of flowers, not of iron. Explain why rules are needed, and discuss them. Teach repair: when something doesn’t work out, look together for what can be fixed, instead of “that’s it, I’m quitting”. There are fewer such children than adults: among those born from 2000 to 2025, one in 27 has 12-16-4.

report: The legend of the 12-16-4 tail argues with itself. In one version, the person held power in a past life and abused it: gave orders, suppressed, controlled. In the other, they were weak, submitted, avoided responsibility — and their life fell apart. Hence the name popular readings give this tail: “the Emperor”. The legend cannot be checked: the numbers say nothing about past events. But its two versions are more accurate than they seem. They are not two different people but **two phases of one circle**.

The clue is written into the cards themselves. The tail begins with the Hanged Man, and Benebell Wen sees a tau cross in his crossed legs — a sign of “the balance between dominion and slavery”. This is the scale 12-16-4 swings on. And among the old names of the Tower, the middle of the tail, Waite lists the Tower of Babel: the figures falling from it are held to be “Nimrod and his minister”. Nimrod, by tradition, is the king who began that tower. None of this is proof: neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the destiny matrix. But the coincidences pile up.

The circle begins not with power but with its opposite: the person holds themselves back. They don’t argue, though they disagree. They don’t ask, though they need to. They don’t leave, though they have long felt cramped. Asked how things are, they say “fine”. In the old description that Waite cites, the Hanged Man’s arms are bound behind him. In Wen, his hands are hidden: “his ultimate offering to the world has yet to be seen”. She calls this state “the unsettling calm before a storm”.

What goes unsaid does not disappear; it builds up. “I’m filing for divorce” over a broken cup. A shout that brings a week of shame. And the partner’s line after the blast: “But you never said anything!” Waite calls the Tower a card “of unforeseen catastrophe”. In this tail, **the catastrophe is unforeseen only by others**.

For Waite, the Tower is the fall of a house built on a false foundation, “a House of Falsehood”. What is false in this house? Our answer: the two phrases it stood on — “I’m fine” and “everything is under control”. The lightning strikes exactly at them. The Tower here does not predict a crash. It describes how change comes: not gradually but all at once, after a long build-up.

The person climbs out from under the rubble with one decision: never like this again. And they build again, harder than before: rules, checks, reserves, everything in their own hands. This is how the root of the tail, the Emperor, works. Wen has an uncomfortable question for this card: “What is the Seeker’s dominion? What has the Seeker conquered? The kingdom is parched.” An order that rests on control alone turns the living into the motionless.

After a collapse comes one of two promises. “Nobody will ever order me around again” — and control turns outwards. “I’ll never lose it like that again” — and the person ties their own hands once more. The promises seem opposite but are made of the same material — power — and both lead to new lightning.

The head of a small team spends three years plugging other people’s gaps and answering every “how are things?” with “fine”. On Friday the director moves his holiday for the third time. On Monday there is a resignation letter on the desk, and everyone is surprised: he never complained. At the new job he sets hard rules from day one: everything goes through him, “I’ve had enough of that once already”. A year later his team sits silent at meetings and answers “how’s it going?” with “fine”. The Tower hasn’t gone anywhere. It has moved, and now other people live in it.

Everyone with 12-16-4 has the same card in the centre of the chart — 8, Strength. This is the method’s arithmetic, and the tail’s formulas read almost like a sentence. Strength is the Emperor plus the Emperor: power turned on oneself. The Hanged Man is the Emperor plus Strength: power over oneself taken as far as tied hands. The Tower is the Emperor plus the Hanged Man: control and restraint give a discharge. The tail is built from the Emperor’s bricks. And in the energy chart, everyone with this tail has Manipura, the row of will, status and money, equal to 8-8-16. **Strength plus Strength is the Tower: self-restraint added to self-restraint gives lightning.**

Waite writes of the woman on the Strength card that “her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers”. Wen puts it more simply: “Compassion is strength.” For her, Strength is mastery over one’s own fears, not over the world around.

What follows is our reading. There are two ways to close a lion’s jaws. The first is to clamp them shut and lock the beast in a tower. That is the path of the Hanged Man, and a lion in a tower grows until it breaks the walls. In the second, the tamed lion walks alongside on a chain of flowers. Anger, desire and will don’t go anywhere: they are heard and led, not strangled. It is the same with people: power rests not on fear but on an agreement accepted with the heart. The key to the tail is not giving up power but changing what it is made of: **an open palm instead of a sceptre**.
In practice, that means three habits:

ul: Say “this doesn’t work for me” within a day — in one sentence, in a calm voice. A small discharge on time replaces a big one three years later.
When tempted to tear everything down, first change one thing this week and set a deadline, so that repair doesn’t turn into more enduring. Decide after the peak of anger, not at it.
Hand over one area completely, along with the right to make mistakes, and stay out of it for a month. The anxiety that raises its head is the lion that needs to be led, not locked up.

report: If there is violence in a relationship, whichever side it comes from, the tail has nothing to do with it. That is a matter for a specialist, and under threat, for those who can protect.

report.h3: Power that people follow without fear

report: A worked-through 12-16-4 holds a structure and knows how to stop and look at things differently. Such people are the best in a crisis: they know collapse from the inside. Their power rests not on fear but on trust: the rules are clear and can be discussed. Even the Tower works for them: Wen writes that its revelation leads not to the end of the road but “to rebuilding and reconstruction”. **They tear down what has outlived itself on their own — piece by piece and on time.**

In Wen’s description, the Emperor’s parched kingdom has a detail that is easy to miss: a small stream runs at the foot of the canyon. Even in the most tightly controlled kingdom, life flows — just down below, under the stones. The work of this tail is not to conquer more land but to let the water through. Then the kingdom won’t need lightning to change.
